oil.summary: Crude gave back a chunk of its recent rally on Wednesday, with WTI off 2.89% to $102.75/bbl and Brent down 2.52% to $105.97, though both retain outsized monthly gains of +21.6% and +16.7% respectively. The session's sharpest move was in RBOB, which cratered 7.04% to $3.22/gal, suggesting demand softness is cutting into refined product premiums even as the supply backdrop stays tense. The headline driver remains the Strait of Hormuz complex: Saudi Arabia's key bypass pipeline is offline, forcing Riyadh to pivot to spot sales near the Strait; Japanese refiners scrambled for Oman crude as an alternative; and Iran-backed Houthi attacks continue to crimp shipping lanes. Iran's stated blockade posture and Trump's escalatory rhetoric add tail-risk. Russia's extension of its diesel export ban through October tightens distillate supply further, while U.S. crude inventories drew a modest 600,000 barrels last week. CME options markets price a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting.
drivers: Saudi Arabia's Hormuz bypass pipeline offline, forcing spot crude sales and triggering Asian refiner scramble for alternative grades
Iran blockade threat and Houthi attacks sustain geopolitical risk premium despite today's profit-taking selloff
Russia extends diesel export ban to end-October, tightening distillate markets even as RBOB demand signals weaken

gas.summary: Henry Hub eased 0.96% to $2.89/MMBtu, a modest pullback within a constructive monthly trend of +7.5%. European TTF fell 3.10% on the day to €77.58/MWh but remains elevated, up 25.6% on the month and still close to 2022 highs per today's headlines. A headline citing TTF at $92.95 intraday underscores intra-session volatility. The key European driver is critically low storage: Germany is actively considering market incentives to encourage restocking ahead of winter. Qatar export disruptions are keeping Atlantic Basin LNG supply tight, prompting Equinor to announce an expansion of its LNG portfolio to 10–15 million tons per year targeting European and Asian buyers. JERA's plan to sell excess LNG in global markets adds a marginal supply offset. Gulf tensions remain a backdrop risk to any LNG re-routing.
drivers: European gas storage at record lows; Germany weighing market incentives to accelerate refill ahead of winter
Qatar LNG exports remain blocked, tightening global LNG supply and prompting Equinor to target 10–15 Mt/year portfolio expansion
JERA plans to sell excess LNG into global markets, providing a partial supply offset to tight Atlantic Basin conditions

power.summary: EU carbon allowances (EUA) dropped 3.90% to $80.53/EUA today, broadly in line with the pullback across energy complex prices. The monthly trend remains modestly positive at +3.5%. The carbon market lacks sector-specific catalysts in today's flow, but the macro backdrop matters: TTF remains near multi-year highs (+25.6% on the month), which elevates gas-fired generation costs and keeps fuel-switching dynamics in focus. A leaked EU Commission draft for RED IV signals a potential shift away from granular hydrogen mandates toward an EU-wide target, which could alter long-run clean-power investment signals. Equinor's LNG expansion and JERA's plans to redistribute supply may gradually ease European gas prices, which would in turn weigh on carbon. Today's data set for power is otherwise thin; no direct power price or grid-level data were provided.
drivers: EUA sold off 3.9% in sympathy with broader energy complex weakness, erasing some of the month's modest gains
Leaked RED IV draft signals potential scrapping of hydrogen mandates in favour of an EU-wide target, shifting clean-energy policy outlook
Persistently elevated TTF prices sustain fuel-switching pressure, but today's 3.1% TTF pullback slightly reduces near-term carbon demand from the power sector
